title: London Court Clears Extradition of Indian-Origin Pharmacist Accused of Arsenic Murder in Hyderabad
excerpt: Ajith Kumar Mupparapu, 46, faces charges of killing his ex-mother-in-law with poisoned spices and plotting to assassinate her father through contract killers and staged accidents.
body:
• A London court ruled that UK-based pharmacist Ajith Kumar Mupparapu, 46, can be extradited to India to face murder and conspiracy charges.
  • Indian prosecutors allege Mupparapu sent arsenic-laced chilli powder and salt to his ex-wife's family in Hyderabad, killing her mother Uma Maheshwari in July 2023.
  • He is also accused of three separate attempts to murder his former father-in-law, including hiring contract killers and staging a road accident.
  • Mupparapu can appeal the ruling at the High Court; his lawyers argued insufficient evidence and the risk of torture in Indian custody.

A British-based pharmacist of Indian origin can be extradited to Hyderabad to stand trial on charges of poisoning his former wife's family with arsenic and repeatedly plotting to kill her father, a London court ruled on September 4, according to Reuters.

Ajith Kumar Mupparapu, 46, is wanted by Telangana authorities in connection with a series of alleged attacks on the family of his ex-wife, Sirisha Muttavarapu, that began in 2023 after the couple separated.

The Arsenic Poisoning

Indian prosecutors allege that Mupparapu arranged for chilli powder and salt contaminated with arsenic to be delivered to the Muttavarapu family's home in Hyderabad. The family consumed meals prepared with the tainted spices while they were gathered for a wedding celebration in June 2023.

https://x.com/TelanganaToday/status/2096240710269993421

Sirisha Muttavarapu's mother, Uma Maheshwari, died the following month. Testing showed arsenic levels in the blood and urine of affected family members were more than 20 times the normal value, according to James Lewis, a lawyer representing Indian prosecutors.

"The evidence showed at least an arguable case against Mupparapu and the Indian authorities had given assurances about his treatment in custody."

— Judge John Zani, Westminster Magistrates' Court

Three Alleged Plots Against the Father-in-Law

The charges extend far beyond the poisoning. Mupparapu is also accused of three separate attempts to murder Muttavarapu's father, Hanumantha Rao: organizing a staged road accident meant to look like a natural crash, attempting to hire contract killers, and conspiring to have him injected with a fatal dose of succinylcholine, a muscle relaxant.

The Crown Prosecution Service, acting on behalf of Indian authorities, told the court that the four incidents — the arsenic conspiracy, the injection plot, the contract killers, and the staged accident — all took place in 2023.

The Defence and Ruling

Mupparapu's lawyers challenged the extradition on two grounds: that there was insufficient direct evidence linking him to the arsenic found at the family's home or proving his involvement in the murder plots, and that he could face torture if sent to India. They cited a February ruling that prevented a businessman from being extradited to India on similar grounds.

Judge John Zani rejected both arguments, finding that the prosecution had established at least an arguable case and accepting assurances from Indian authorities regarding Mupparapu's treatment in custody.

What Happens Next

Mupparapu can appeal the decision at the High Court. His lawyer did not comment on the ruling. He has not been convicted of any of the charges. If no successful appeal is mounted, the case will proceed toward extradition to India, where he would face trial in Hyderabad.

For the Indian diaspora in the UK, the case underscores the reach of Indian law enforcement in pursuing cross-border criminal allegations and the growing use of extradition treaties to bring suspects back to face trial.
nri_angle: The case highlights the cross-border legal exposure faced by members of the Indian diaspora in the UK and the effectiveness of extradition treaties between India and Britain.
